extracted.intended_audience: architects, students of architecture, architectural critics, and designers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines about truthfulness, material honesty, decoration, and craft in architectural design — emphasizing honest materials, hand-work, avoidance of trickery, and the proper use of color and ornament. Drawn from aesthetic and moral principles for building and ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: False representation of material is base and inadmissible
rubrics_metrics.description: “All such imitations are utterly base and inadmissible.” Imitations of one material as another (e.g., marbling shop fronts, imitation granite, painted stucco pretending to stone) are morally and aesthetically wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: marbled shop fronts, imitation granite at the British Museum landing, false marble in churches. Such imitations waste resources, mislead the eye, and undermine trust in material honesty. They do not add comfort or cleanliness or true conspicuousness and are condemned especially in high architecture and in places of worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church furniture must be simple, unaffected, and pure
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first condition which just feeling requires in church furniture is, that it should be simple and unaffected, not fictitious nor tawdry.” Religious furnishings should avoid faux finishes and tawdry ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer solid stone and solid wood, even whitewashed for cleanliness; simple village churches built roughly of stone and wood are often free from offensive ugliness. Reject smoothly stuccoed walls, gilded or bronzed wood, painted iron, wretched upholstery, Birmingham metal candlesticks, and 'the green and yellow sickness of the false marble.' Such falsities are obstacles to devotional repose and erode moral taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pretend — whatever is pretended is wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever is pretended, is wrong.” Concealment that asserts a false reality is blameworthy; finishes that honestly show themselves are less objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitewash is allowable because it 'shows itself for what it is' and does not assert the nature of what's beneath. Gilding, understood as a mere film and not claiming to be solid gold, is allowable though often abused. The guiding test: does the surface assert an untrue substance or quality?

rubrics_metrics.name: Veneering acceptable only if not deceptive; prefer substantial materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble facing (veneering) can be legitimate if it does not 'pretend or imply a marble wall' and when precious stones cannot be used solidly; but there is a preference for walls of 'noble substance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat veneering as a large-scale mosaic — durable and sometimes necessary — but balance the two principles of Sacrifice and Truth: sometimes better to spare external ornament than to diminish real substance. Consciousness of thoroughness in substance leads to better design and more studious decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve painting and transient coloring until durable qualities secured
rubrics_metrics.description: External colour and painted decoration are 'not less true' but essentially unarchitectural and should be subsidiary to enduring fabric; the painter's work should be reserved for shadowed loggia and inner chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stained and variegated stone where possible; for bright colors, use glass and gold protected by glass (mosaic) since mosaics are as durable as stone. Beware that painted aids will pass away and a building will be judged in its 'lifelessness'—prefer less bright, more enduring fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute rejection of substitution of cast/machine work for hand (Operative Deceit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operative Deceit: substituting cast or machine-made ornament for hand-work is both bad as work and dishonest; it is 'a downright and inexcusable lie.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hand-wrought ornament carries the record of human labour and care; using machine-made substitutes pretends a worth that is not present. The author advises absolute and unconditional rejection of such deception, preferring bare walls or honest simple materials rather than false ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and moral worth of hand-wrought ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The delight in ornament stems from the consciousness of 'human labor and care spent upon it.' Hand-work records thought, trial, and success and confers worth beyond mere material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even materials inferior in intrinsic quality (e.g., a hand-wrought terra cotta) can surpass machine-cut noble stone in value if the hand has been evident. The touch of human workmanship is essential to ornament's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable exceptions for moulded/formed materials (brick, tile, porcelain)
rubrics_metrics.description: For materials known to be moulded (brick, tile, porcelain), cast or moulded forms may be legitimately and successfully used because they do not pretend to be cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited positive examples: brick mouldings of Palazzo Pepoli (Bologna) and Vercelli, coloured tiles in French domestic architecture, Robbia porcelain bas-reliefs in Tuscany. The rule: do not make moulded materials pretend to be carved stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use artificial stone or stucco to mimic carved stone
rubrics_metrics.description: Stucco ornaments and artificial stones cast into shape which might be mistaken for real stone are condemned as dishonest and degrading (example: stucco mouldings in the cortile of the Palazzo Vecchio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stone is normally expected to be carved by hand, using cast or artificial imitations that might be mistaken for it casts 'shame and suspicion' over the building. The material's expected mode of manufacture should be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast iron ornament: honest but aesthetically degrading
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast iron work, though often distinguishable from wrought iron and therefore 'honest,' is 'cold, clumsy, and vulgar,' and degrades national taste when indulged in as a cheap substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not dishonest, cast iron lacks the capacity for fine line or shadow and should never be employed in places where it would attain the credit of better work or be associated with 'downright' hand-work; it gives little hope for artistic progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disdain display of dexterity and architectural sleight-of-hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid tricks and vanities that display dexterity and ingenious device; they tend to catch uninventive architects and feelingless spectators and can 'draw us away from all regard and care for the nobler character of the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against subtle deceptions by cultivating a 'manly and unaffected spirit' and dedicate creative effort to arrangement of masses and forms rather than clever surface devices. Stern disdain for display of technical dexterity is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect structural and material truth: stone must read as stone (mass before line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute the line for the mass in a way that denies the material's qualities: stone is 'stiff' and should not be represented as ductile or elastic; representing it as if it were a woven net or silken cord is a 'deliberate treachery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transition from focus on light (openings) to fixation on tracery lines led to a decline when tracery was reduced to hair-like bars and treated as flexible. Designs must reflect the true mechanical and visual qualities of their materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid penetrable/penetrated tracery and intersectional moulding falsities
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing mouldings and tracery as penetrable (one appearing to pass through another) or managing intersections to exhibit dexterity is a form of falsity that 'crushed the art' and led to decline in Gothic architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier practice kept mouldings coincident or simply managed; later devices created under- and emergent forms and intersections as displays of technical skill. Such intersectional mouldings are criticised; the architecture should not be based on tricks of intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When inventiveness leads to structural awkwardness, prefer simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The awkwardness with which early builders met difficult junctions (keeping them simple and shaded) is praised; the later habit of emphasizing complex intersections attracted the eye to technical artifice rather than to proportion and mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a junction or moulding produces uncomfortable visual or structural effects, it is better to avoid exposing it; simplicity and unwillingness to attract the eye to awkward arrangements maintain dignity of style. Decorative invention must not undermine the larger design.
